**Article Details for PMID: 42608275**

**Title:** On-target and off-target activities of CRISPR therapeutics across scales.

**Authors:** Merna Magdy, Justin R Gibson, Abishek Dhungana, Ashley Herring-Nicholas, Renee N Cottle, Eric A Josephs

**Journal:** Trends in biotechnology
**Publication Date:** 2026-08-29
**DOI:** 10.1016/j.tibtech.2026.07.015
**PMC ID:** 13509143
**Full Text Available:** Yes
**Full Text URL:** https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13509143/


**Abstract:**
Recent FDA-approved gene-editing therapies illustrate not only the transformative potential of biotechnologies using CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats)-derived ribonucleoproteins in treating a broad range of diseases but also the spectrum of possible molecular variations CRISPR therapeutics can adopt. These include exagamglogene autotemcel, an ex vivo therapy for hemoglobinopathies using CRISPR nuclease Cas9, and kayjayguran abengcemeran, an in vivo therapy using a protospacer adjacent motif-altered base-editing Cas9 variant for an ultra-rare metabolic disorder. Together, these therapies underscore how far CRISPR has advanced beyond its original use as a tool in biological/biomedical research. In this opinion article, we argue that as CRISPR biotechnologies advance beyond the relative simplicity of in vitro applications, our understanding must also evolve to address the challenges of optimizing 'on-target' and 'off-target' mutational activities across the diverse contexts in which they occur.

**Full Text:**
Correspondence: rcottle@clemson.edu (R.N. Cottle) and Eric.Josephs@stonybrook.edu (E.A. Josephs).

Recent FDA-approved gene editing therapies illustrate not only the transformative potential of CRISPR biotechnologies in treating a broad range of diseases but also the spectrum of possible molecular variations CRISPR therapeutics can adopt. These include exagamglogene autotemcel, an ex vivo Cas9-mediated therapy for hemoglobinopathies, and kayjayguran abengcemeran, an in vivo therapy using a PAM-altered, base-editing Cas9 variant for an ultra-rare metabolic disorder. Together, these therapies underscore how far CRISPR has advanced beyond its original use as a tool in biological/biomedical research. Here, we argue that as CRISPR biotechnologies advance beyond the relative simplicity of in vitro applications, our understanding must also evolve to address the challenges of optimizing “on-target” and “off-target” mutational activities across the diverse contexts in which they occur.

Keywords: Cas9, precision genetic medicine (PGM), N-of-1, inherited genetic disease, specificity

“The fox knows many things, but the hedgehog knows one big thing.” Archilochus, Fragments, as quoted in The Hedgehog and the Fox (1953) by Isaiah Berlin

The field of medicine is experiencing a revolutionary shift in treating genetic diseases. Since the FDA’s first approvals of CRISPR therapeutics [1–3] — where ribonucleoprotein (RNP) (see Glossary) complexes consisting of bacterially derived CRISPR-associated (Cas) enzymes and guide RNAs (gRNAs) are used to make changes to DNA at specific sequences to alleviate disease symptoms — there is now a strong movement by the US government and industry to significantly broaden the use of CRISPR biotechnologies to treat many different chronic conditions [4].

The most widely used CRISPR gene editing tools consist of the Cas9 nuclease from Streptococcus pyogenes (Figure 1) to target double-stranded DNA sequences matching the modular “spacer” segment of the gRNA, provided the target site lies immediately 5’- of an ‘NGG’ protospacer adjacent motif (PAM). When introduced into human cells, Cas9 generates double-strand breaks (DSBs) in target sequences specified by base pairing on the complementary strand with the spacer. These DSBs are repaired by erroneous cellular mechanisms like non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), resulting in permanent sequence alterations: typically, insertions and deletions (indels) that can result in frameshift mutations and disrupt gene function. The programmability of the CRISPR system makes it immensely powerful as an editor – it can be redirected to different sequences in the cell’s genome by simply changing the gRNA’s spacer region – which has driven its widespread adoption in biomedical research, enabling applications ranging from streamlined forward-genetic approaches like genome-wide knockout screens [5,6] to reverse-genetic approaches with targeted gene knockout, which can also be used in the early stages of gene therapy development to rapidly identify CRISPR RNPs able to improve disease phenotypes at the cellular level and that themselves might represent promising therapeutic leads themselves.

A) Contrasting requirements of CRISPR biotechnologies for biomedical and biological research applications and their use as “bespoke” therapeutics for genetic disorders. B) Schematic illustration of how the meanings of “on-target” and “off-target”, commonly used in characterizing CRISPR activity, vary across scales from the molecular level to the patient level. Abbreviations: PAM: protospacer adjacent motif; gRNA: guide RNA; RNP: ribonucleoprotein.

During the infancy of CRISPR biotechnologies, significant efforts went into engineering the CRISPR RNP to extend its capabilities as a tool for biomedical research (Figure 2). These include amino acid changes to Cas9s’ PAM- and target-recognition domains to fine-tune their abilities to recognize different genomic loci, particularly by loosening PAM requirements to increase the number of targets that are recognized [5–8]; fusing chimeric domains to Cas9 to expand the spectrum of DNA modifications that could be introduced [9–11], such as precise nucleotide changes without DSBs for base editing and prime editing, or to interact with cellular DNA damage repair (DDR) machinery to enhance mutagenic efficiencies; and modifications to the gRNA itself to attenuate the interaction of the RNP with different DNA sequences. In silico tools that help to predict biochemical activity and mutagenic outcomes at different target sequences [12–16] were also developed to accelerate the experimental workflow [13,17]. However, now that the same biomolecules are being directly adapted for use as therapeutics themselves, the engineering design constraints for those RNPs have begun to diverge significantly from those earlier directions (Figure 1A); whereas “modularity” and “speed” are key for biomedical research, instead “safety” and “efficacy” are of paramount importance for the therapeutic being developed, and those attributes will need to be specifically defined within their particular therapeutic context and within the context of a patient’s unique genome.

A) Examples of different molecular variations of the Cas9 enzyme and gRNA that have been developed to optimize their potential for specific therapeutic targets: choice of Cas9 variant (yellow); enzyme variants with amino acid substitutions in their nuclease (orange), DNA interacting or PAM-recognition domains (green); chimeric domains (pink) to introduce chemical modifications to nucleotides within the R-loop; reverse transcriptase to extend a nicked strand using a 3’ extension of the gRNA, or modulators of endogenous DNA damage repair pathways (turquoise); and other small changes to the enzyme like inclusion of nuclear localization factors. The modifications to the sequence or chemical modifications to the gRNA within the spacer sequence (red), additional segments 5’- of the spacer sequence (blue), or extended 3’- the primary gRNA sequence (e.g. pegRNAs, light green) can also be performed. B) Cas9 RNPs with spacers for different targets (dashed lines, determined by the presence of adjacent PAMs) will exhibit significantly different biochemical activities at their intended targets (represented by arrows pointing toward DNA) in ways that can be difficult to predict ab initio. Because the propensity of a Cas9 RNP to also become activated even at sequences that don’t match their spacer depends on the location, species, and context of the mismatched nucleotides, each Cas9 with a different RNP will also have a different spectrum of potential mutagenic activities at unintended “off-target” sequences (represented by arrows pointing away from the DNA) that must be quantified and minimized. C) An emerging strategy to optimize precise gene editing efficiencies for a specific target sequence (orange circle) using a bespoke base editor involves, first, evaluating a large number of candidate spacers overlapping the target using a PAM-less Cas9 variant for editing efficiency. Once a promising spacer has been identified, a PAM-stringent Cas9 variant that recognizes a personalized PAM sequence immediately 3’ of the target, closely matched to the target site, can be substituted to enhance target recognition and editing activity for clinical application. D) The desired functional or therapeutic change – a gene knockout; a targeted disruption of a specific sequence of interest (i.e., an aberrant splice site or transcription factor enhancer/recognition site); base editing of a specific nucleotide; base editing change resulting in knockout (i.e., mutation to introduce an aberrant mRNA splice site); or prime editing to introduce specific insertions, deletions, or substitutions at a genomic site – limits the number of possible spacer sequences available for a CRISPR RNP, which in turn is limited by the presence of nearby PAM sequences. The ability to achieve the different mutational outcomes required to achieve those changes are attenuated (or potentially enhanced) by different DNA damage repair (DDR) pathways that may be differentially active in the specific type of cell that needs to be edited, depending on factors like senescence / replicative potential. NHEJ: non-homologous end joining (DSB repair). HDR: homology directed repair (DSB repair). FA: Fanconi anemia DNA damage repair pathway. MMR: DNA mismatch repair pathway. BER: base excision repair, NER: nucleotide excision repair.

In 2025, a personalized CRISPR base-editing therapeutic designed for a single patient with severe carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS1) deficiency, a rare genetic condition, was delivered into a neonate within the first few months after their birth [3]. Comparing that treatment (kayjayguran abengcemeran; k-abe) [3,18] with the CRISPR therapeutic for sickle cell disease (SCD) and β-thalassemia (TDT), the first CRISPR therapy approved by the FDA in 2023 (exagamglogene autotemcel; exa-cel or CASGEVY) [2,19], reveals the significant specialization required to adapt Cas9, a biomedical and biological research tool, for its specific therapeutic applications. While both use derivatives of the same Cas9, CASGEVY is delivered ex vivo using a Cas9 RNP for a common inherited disease in adolescents and adults, whereas k-abe is delivered in vivo as a personalized N-of-1 therapy for a newborn using a base editor with a PAM-altered variant of Cas9.

These clinical milestones reflect the transformation of the CRISPR from “foxes” – reprogrammable molecular tools used to introduce mutations into targeted DNA – to “hedgehogs”, representing highly specialized, therapeutic RNPs optimized for treatment of a specific genetic disease. Common terminology used to describe the activities of Cas9 in earlier applications of biotechnology, such as “on-target” or “off-target” mutational effects [20], has now taken on varying meanings depending on context and modality during therapeutic development and treatment. The nuances of these terms vary as the focus shifts from the molecular to the cellular, organ and tissue, and patient- and population-level scales (Figure 1B). Here, we explore how these definitions vary in meaning across spatial and temporal scales within the CRISPR therapeutic design process (Box 1), while highlighting bottlenecks, overlooked areas, and emerging opportunities at each level.

When considering meaning of the common terminology used for characterizing CRISPR biotechnologies—”on-target efficiency”, “off-target efficiency”, “specificity”—mean with regards to therapeutics, it is important to be precise in our language and what aspect of the CRISPR therapeutic we are evaluating.

At the biomolecular level, the “targeting space” of a CRISPR RNP in general (with any spacer sequence) describes the biochemical activity at desired or unwanted DNA sequences occurring as a result of biochemical properties of the Cas9 RNPs. This would include how Cas9 variants with different PAM-recognition domains will have different spectra of possible homologous sequences in a genome; how different Cas9 variants (like high-fidelity engineered Cas9) with different amino acids that alter the affinity of the enzyme for DNA, and/or have different tolerances to different mismatched base-pair context-, species-, or position within the R-loop; variants that impact cellular or nuclear delivery in the specific cell type of interest; or how different base editing Cas9 variants might have different propensities for intended or bystander mutations at different positions within the R-loop.

We next consider the CRISPR “editing window” to be the domain at which improvements or current limitations in the ability to introduce cellular or biologically functional changes as well as phenotypical alterations. The editing window describes the behavior of the set of possible CRISPR RNPs able to introduce the genetic alterations capable of treating a specific genetic disease. Effectiveness varies between cell types, which impacts how well edits result in functional or phenotypic modifications and highlights the challenge of preventing unwanted mutations from CRISPR RNPs. For each type of desired mutation, there is only a finite number of existing spacer sequences of a gRNA that are capable of directing a Cas9 effector to the genomic sequences where that edit may be possible.

So, at this scale, we would consider for a given Cas9 RNP: (1) how efficiently its normally-innate biochemical activity is triggered at its intended target in the cell type of interest; (2) how likely mutations at different loci that are similar to the target occur both at the cell type of interest and other cell types that might be exposed to the Cas9 variant; and (3) how likely the biochemical activity generated by the CRISPR effector results in the desired mutation within different cell types exposed to the effector. These are different kinds of considerations than required for “genome-wide knockout” gRNA library design, for example.

To define the CRISPR “mutagenic efficiency”, we are concerned about improvements or current limitations in the ability of a specific CRISPR RNP to practically be delivered to and generate the desired mutations within the environments of the specific tissues, organs, or organ systems required to treat a disease. This term takes into consideration controlling the delivery and lifespan of CRISPR RNPs across both “space” (bio-distribution) and “time” (how long they are in the cells of interest). And ultimately, in the context of CRISPR “treatment effectiveness”, the focus is on improvements or current limitations to generate sufficient genetic mutations in the intended targets (in vivo or ex vivo) that are persistent enough to treat a disease, or potentially have side-effects, in individual patients as well as larger patient populations. The evaluation of “mutagenic efficiency” directly plays into “treatment effectiveness, warranting consideration of the molecular identity of unwanted sequence targeting across different patients and patient populations, and their distribution and persistence in the body, and whether they might contribute to disease over the years of clinical observation and patient lifetime.

In contrast to earlier editors like TALENs and ZFNs, which require protein engineering to change their DNA targets [21], CRISPR technologies can be redirected with a simple change of the gRNA alone. Regardless, numerous modifications have been made to the original S. pyogenes Cas9 enzyme during its development as a biotechnology tool to expand its “targeting space” (Figure 2A and Box 1). How useful these modifications are in practice depends on whether they are to be used for biomedical and biological research applications or as therapeutics.

An inherent challenge of CRISPR systems is that the actual biochemical activity of a CRISPR RNP can vary significantly depending on the specific sequence targeted [22], often quite unpredictably (Figure 2B). In addition to variations that result from differences in the spacer sequence, the most significant factor in CRISPR activity is encoded in the amino acids of the Cas9 protein itself for the recognition of a set of PAM sequences, without which there is extremely limited CRISPR activity. The requirement of an ‘NGG’ PAM (or a less efficient ‘NAG’ PAM) immediately 3’ to a sequence of interest inherently limits the number of sites where Cas9 could induce a desired mutation. Hence, significant efforts were made to engineer “nearly PAM-less” Cas9 variants, with relaxed PAM requirements recognizing ‘NR’ motifs (R = A or G) and, with slightly lower affinity, ‘NY’ (Y = T or C) PAMs, to expand the number of spacers that can be evaluated [6,7]. However, these variants exhibit significantly lower enzymatic rates and gene-editing activity than variants with more stringent PAMs [6,23]. Recently, there has been a trend toward generating a menagerie of PAM-altered Cas9 variants that recognize distinct but specific PAM sites [24–26]. A new strategy for developing bespoke CRISPR therapies is emerging that involves, in the early-stage discovery, using PAM-less Cas9 variants to evaluate a large number of candidate spacers, then switching to a PAM-restricted Cas9 variant that recognizes a “bespoke” PAM closely matched to the target DNA for the clinical application (Figure 2C); this approach was used in developing k-abe [3].

As alluded to above, a major challenge in the development of CRISPR biotechnologies has been that these enzymes can also be activated at unwanted sequences that are similar to, but do not exactly match, their intended targets [27–29] — what have been historically called “off-target” sequences (Figure 2B). This even includes mutagenic single-strand breaks (nicking) [30] that occur during base editing and prime editing. Different CRISPR effectors have varying tolerance to activation, depending on the specific mismatches, sequence context, and the positions of those mismatches within the spacer [31]. For example, the S. pyogenes Cas9 can cleave sequences divergent from the intended targets with as many as 6 – 8 mismatches within the 20 nt protospacer region. Even with the help of computational tools, activity at these genetically similar sequences is difficult to predict [32], let alone control. To address this challenge, engineered “high-fidelity” Cas9 (hfCas9) variants with modified amino acids in their target recognition domains have been developed to reduce that activity. But these modifications also decrease the overall binding affinity between Cas9 and DNA, thereby attenuating gene-editing efficiency at the intended as well as the unintended sequences [33,34]. While this attenuation can be tolerated in early studies, where Cas9 is typically overexpressed, it may limit their therapeutic efficacy. Additionally, hfCas9 variants may not fully eliminate gene editing at all unintended sequences present in a patient’s genome. As a result, for therapeutic applications, stringent nomination (identification of genomic sequences similar to the target) and experimental quantification of unwanted mutagenic activity at those sites must always be performed [35,36].

In the case of genome-wide screens, experiments are simplified by using a single hfCas9 variant for large numbers of gRNAs. But perhaps there is an opportunity, analogous to the shift from “nearly PAMless” to “bespoke PAM” Cas9 variants during therapeutic development: In those therapeutic applications, typically only a single, prescribed gRNA is used, and the specific potential sites of unwanted activity have already been identified in vitro. Under those conditions, there may be other combinations of amino acid changes [33,35,36] and gRNA variants [37–39] (within or outside the spacer) that can be identified for that specific target of interest to eliminate potential interactions with those specific validated and unwanted sequences — optimized for efficient catalytic activity but only at the one intended target. In other words, once a therapeutic target has been identified, there is no longer a strong need for Cas9’s modularity, and target-specific RNP variants, engineered both at the level of the gRNA and the enzyme itself (Figure 2A), could be swapped in: particularly if the RNP is delivered as RNA, since minor edits can be made within the same therapeutic-grade RNA manufacturing pipeline. Because the safety and effectiveness of each precision genetic medicine (PGM) (combination of gRNA, effector, and delivery modality) must be demonstrated before use, why remain bound to the original Cas9 enzyme used during the initial discovery phase of therapeutic development when better RNP variants might exist for that specific target?

RNPs with different spacer sequences will each exhibit varying sequence-dependent activities [40] that generally do not follow simple design rules [41], and each will have different numbers and varieties of similar sequences present in a patient’s genome that it can also potentially mutate (Figure 2B). Therefore, “specificity” must be defined precisely within the context of a specific therapeutic gRNA design, or across the number of possible candidate gRNAs for a given target (its “editing window”; Figure 3A inset). The editing window is determined by: (i) the presence of PAMs that are (ii) located close enough to a genetic sequence such that (iii) the spectrum of possible biochemical activities that occur as a result of CRISPR recognition (iv) can yield a sufficient variety of mutational events to achieve a therapeutic outcome (Figures 2D and 3A; Box 1).

A) CRISPR as a versatile gene editing biotechnology can be rapidly repurposed to explore the “editing window” of a genetic disease (top right corner) and efficiently identify gene editing therapeutic candidates with high mutagenic efficiencies and therapeutic effectiveness. B) Once the basis of those gene editing therapies is found, are there opportunities for them to serve as a jumping off point to develop “bespoke modifications” to the RNP: can the specific RNP (Cas9 effector and gRNA outside the spacer) be further optimized for activity and specificity just for that intended target? How than this framework be extended to treat related genetic diseases with potentially rare or unique pathogenic genetic variants, or even personalized for safety on the basis on a patient’s unique DNA?

The spectrum of possible targets in the development of a CRISPR therapeutic is dictated by the pathobiology of the genetic variations, and could span a “narrowly-tailored” window of targets (the CRISPR RNP needs to engage with a specific variation and no others, and so typically it must be different for each pathogenic variations) to a larger set of “one-size-fits-all” targets (the same CRISPR RNP can be used to diseases caused by a large number of pathogenic variations) (Figure 3A inset). Examples of “narrowly-tailored” therapies might include the direct base editing modification to eliminate the deleterious stop codon that causes the CPS1 deficiency treated by k-abe; while examples of “one-size-fits-all” might be represented by those that disrupt other genetic features that are located either downstream or upstream of the disease variation, such as exa-cel which by virtue of its mechanism (mutating a regulator for the expression of different hemoglobin genes) is therapeutic for a large number of genetically-related but distinct hemoglobinopathies. “One-size-fits-all” approaches might also be applicable, for example, in metabolic disorders where many individual variations across few genes result in a build-up of a toxic metabolite, so that targeted disruption of another gene in the metabolic pathway can yield a therapeutic benefit; hence large numbers of possible targets across potentially multiple genes can be evaluated for efficacy and safety.

A special case of “narrowly-tailored” editing windows involves the allele-specific targeting of a single-nucleotide variation (SNV) on a single chromosome, which can cause many genetic diseases (e.g., autosomal dominant ones) for which CRISPR-based knockout of only the pathogenic variant might result in a therapeutic benefit. But even hfCas9 variants are unable to differentiate between such small differences at present. Currently, the most reliable method to differentiate between SNVs on different chromosomes is if the pathogenic variant results in a novel PAM sequence (such as a pathogenic SNV that introduces a new NGG motif) [43]. Advances in Cas9 PAM engineering [24–26] could open new possibilities for SNVs to be recognized as novel PAMs occurring on one chromosome, although they might be limited if there are no effective spacers to pair with that PAM.

Along the another axis in the editing design space (Figure 3A inset) is whether a specific mutagenic outcome is required (“tightly-controlled”) or not (“mutationally permissive”). Mutationally permissive therapeutics will typically involve the Cas9 nuclease, such that the DSBs it induces at a target result in stochastic indels; or use a base editing Cas9 to create aberrant splice sites (as treatments for high cholesterol, targeting PCSK9) without DSBs. If the purpose is to disrupt a recognition sequence (exa-cel) or a specific gene via frameshift (as in CRISPR therapeutics for ATTR), then as long as the target is sufficiently disrupted – it doesn’t matter exactly how – then that can suffice for therapeutic benefit (Figure 2D). However, because DNA repair of DSBs is a stochastic process, it can result in in-frame indels (which may preserve partial function) or larger, more deleterious chromosomal rearrangements; there is an increasing trend to first identify target knockouts using the nucleolytic Cas9, then for therapeutic applications replace those knock-out protocols with base editing to introduce inactivating mutations or premature stop codons into those genes without DSBs [44,45], if possible.

For diseases requiring tight control over mutational outcomes (Figure 2D), these edits can be achieved using: (1) allelic replacement with nucleolytic targeting within ~100 bp of the variation of interest, but which can also result in indels at the target site. (2) Base editing to correct a specific mutation, such that the R-loop must have the variant of interest within the segment of the protospacer at a position where efficient chemical modification of the nucleotide can occur; different base-editing Cas9 variants have different windows within the R-loop where chemical modification is most likely. Included in that category might be whether or not bystander mutations [9,46,47] during base editing can be limited to only synonymous mutations while correcting a pathogenic variation; in some cases [48], that cannot be attained even after evaluating many different base editor variants. (3) Prime editing using a prime editor guide RNA (pegRNA) optimized at both the spacer sequence and the 3’ end containing the reverse transcriptase template sequence.

Gene-editing outcomes are mediated by diverse cellular DNA damage repair (DDR) mechanisms [50] with variable activities across cell types even from the same tissue [49], depending on several factors, including cell cycle status. While DDR mechanisms in cell lines or immortalized cells are relatively well understood, significant gaps remain in our knowledge of these mechanisms in many primary cells, and there is increasing evidence that Cas9 activity differs even between cell lines and related primary cells. Further, the mechanisms of DDR-mediated editing in non-proliferating cells and how they can be exploited to enhance therapeutic editing efficiencies is an area of limited understanding: a recent study highlights this gap [51]. This is also true of other diverse DDR mechanisms that influence base editing and prime editing [14] (Figure 2D). In certain primary cells, it can be significantly more difficult to obtain the amount of data required for AI/ML-based predictive models of CRISPR activity and mutational outcomes. These models could be supplemented by higher-throughput in vitro screens [52] that might serve as Bayesian priors during model training while reducing the experimental burden.

In a recent study [53], a genome-wide CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) screen identified several homologous recombination- (HR)- associated proteins and novel factors that could be chimerically fused to a Cas9 effector to improve allelic replacement in human pluripotent stem cells and Cas9-mediated knock-in of chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) primary human T cells, both mediated by the HR (Figure 2D). Further, the development of cell-specific Cas9 RNPs could be useful across a spectrum of diseases affecting specific tissue types. There could be significant opportunities in generating Cas9 chimeras (Figure 2A) that are optimized for a specific cell-type, biochemical activity modality, and desired mutational outcome in their eventual tissue.

Across tissues and organs, risk cannot be assessed solely by focusing on sequence homology between the intended target and any similar sequences alone, but also through an expanded evaluation of the therapeutic’s (i) bio-distribution and delivery requirements; (ii) whether the CRISPR effector can access those intended sequences in the presence of cell-specific epigenetic factors [54], and (iii) other cell- and tissue- specific effects (Figure 1B).

While ex vivo cell-based approaches allow for rigorous quality control prior to reimplantation in the patient, there are emerging opportunities for PGMs that operate in vivo by optimizing delivery, dosage, and other physiological factors to help reduce the risks of pathogenic mutations [49]. A major strategy involves shifting the burden of “specificity” from the RNP itself by controlling organ-specific delivery. Adeno-associated viral vectors (AAVs) have been the most widely used delivery system for introducing CRISPR nucleases into animal models, owing to their superior tissue tropism, including AAV9 for targeting the central nervous system (CNS). The primary challenge with using AAVs for gene editing is the constitutive expression of the CRISPR system from the AAV vector. Continuous expression of Cas9 effectors over months increases the probability of unwanted edits or translocation events even at low-affinity genomic sites. The transition from AAV to other delivery modalities [60–63], most notably lipid nanoparticles (LNP), is largely driven by the need for better temporal control of Cas9 RNP activity in target cells and tissue [64]. Furthermore, pre-existing adaptive immunity excludes significant patient populations from AAV therapies and redosing. LNP formulations solve these challenges through a transient kinetic profile by delivering editors as mRNA or RNP rather than DNA, so that the editor can act on its target, but degraded rapidly before interrogating lower-affinity loci [20]. Furthermore, LNPs eliminate the risks of Cas9-induced viral vector integration into DSBs and potential insertional mutagenesis associated with AAV delivery [65].

Efforts to tune lipid chemistry to achieve organ-specific targeting, including for tissue types that are difficult to transfect such as the CNS, are ongoing. For example, in developing therapies for transthyretin amyloidosis [66] or hypercholesterolemia [67,68], safety profiles were enhanced using LNPs with liver-restricted tropism. Taken together, for a given spacer (Figure 2B), while mutation at unwanted sequences in relatively high-affinity loci for a CRISPR RNP may exist in a patient’s genome, the clinical relevance of mutation at those sites may be limited if the delivery vehicle physically excludes the editor from tissues where those loci are functionally critical and significantly lowers the risks of pathology from those mutations.

An additional critical consideration for in vivo editing is the target organ’s regenerative capacity. In post-mitotic tissues like the CNS [69] or heart [70], significant unwanted DNA DSBs can elicit apoptosis with the potential to cause permanent organ damage. In contrast, the liver is highly regenerative such that if an aberrant editing activity results in cellular toxicity, the affected hepatocyte is likely cleared and replaced by a healthy hepatocyte that is stimulated to replicate, but a consequence can be the proliferation of oncogenic mutations. Balancing these principles likely contributed to FDA’s streamlined approach to allow k-abe, with a shift in the regulatory focus from requiring the elimination of all unwanted potential mutations (one such site was identified during development but determined to be unlikely to be oncogenic) to a risk-benefit analysis of the potential consequence of mutations [3].

Where multiple different cell types can be impacted, Cas9 edits can create unique liabilities, particularly for treatment of hematologic diseases. For example, given the complex logistics required for ex vivo CAR-T and hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) therapies [71], there is a recent push toward in vivo administration [72,73]. However, systemic delivery into these target cell types bypasses ex vivo quality control and introduces acute risks associated with unintended edits that could drive clonal expansion and off-tissue organ transfection. Inadvertent transfection of B-cells or HSPCs can lead to unintended lineage expression or oncogenic transformation. A critical failure mode unique to in vivo delivery is the accidental transduction of malignant cells, which may express the CAR construct and effectively mask the tumor from the engineered immune response. The tolerance for this type of unwanted activity in vivo is critically low in hematopoietic lineages due to the founder effect of clonal ancestors. A single carcinogenic mutation within an HSPC is permanently imprinted on its entire clonal lineage. This permanence is a primary hurdle for in vivo strategies like fetal hemoglobin reactivation for sickle cell disease, where both therapeutic and genotoxic edits are inherited by the entire erythroid lineage. Given these significant hurdles and tight regulatory oversight, gene editing in the hematopoietic system should remain an ex vivo approach until the field can guarantee the same level of lineage-specific precision in vivo that is currently achieved ex vivo, where scalability and safety are well established. Further, clinical trials for specific cell types including chondrocytes, retinal epithelial cells, and keratinocytes have shown promising outcomes and provide confidence for the future of ex vivo based therapies.

For diseases afflicting other organs, the main constraint is accessibility of target cells rather than the regenerative capacity. In lungs afflicted by cystic fibrosis, for example, delivery strategies must therefore focus on mucus-penetrating [74] particles delivered via nebulization to reach protected stem cell niches. Here, the predominant determinant of activity is accessibility. Because it is mechanically difficult to deliver cargo to basal cells, the systemic effective concentration of Cas9 is negligible following inhalation [75]. Thus, the potential toxicity in this case is locally confined.

The duration of CRISPR RNPs across different spatial and temporal scales is another critical factor for ensuring the editor kinetics match the regenerative, immune, and accessibility profiles of the target organ. At the level of PGM, the effectiveness is determined not just by the fraction of cells in the targeted tissue with the desired edit, but also the question of persistence of the edited cells over time. Depending on the nature of the disease, edited cells may exhibit a fitness advantage [60] over those harboring pathogenic mutations, and, in the case of exa-cel [2], the therapeutic effect can last for at least 4 years. Similarly, there is a risk that sufficient threshold numbers of cells edited at unwanted sequences may have pathogenic or oncogenic effects [61–63]. These two competing factors, along with the severity and rate of disease progression, weigh into timing and the number of doses of PGMs delivered [20].

Pre-existing immunity to common Cas9 orthologs, often derived from human pathogenic or commensal bacteria (e.g., S. pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus), is widespread, with up to 78% of individuals possessing anti-Cas9 antibodies and Cas9-specific T cells [80]. Detrimental effects from Cas9 immunity, including elimination of Cas9-expressing cells by cytotoxic T cells, can lead to loss of gene-edited cells and organ damage [81,82]. In an effort to generate CRISPR effectors unlike any seen in nature, Cas9-like gene editors have been generated using AI models, differing by >40% at the amino acid level from other known Cas9s, with the best-performing effector, termed OpenCRISPR-1, lacking known antigenic epitopes [83].

Each patient will possess non-pathogenic genetic variations. These variations were found to be of clinical relevance in the case of exa-cel [64,65]: even though no editing at nominated off-target sequences was observed in vitro [65], an in silico analysis later revealed that a significant proportion of individuals of African ancestry have a non-pathogenic SNV (rs114518452), introducing a novel NGG PAM for a protospacer that differs from the intended target by only 3 nt. Mutagenic activity at this site was validated in vitro using the exa-cel RNP [64]. While that specific sequence variant was not observed in the initial cohort of patients, this finding highlights the importance of personalized risk assessment at the level of a patient’s individual genome using molecular techniques to nominate all potential off-target sites to ensure safety, but also suggests further improvements to the CRISPR RNP that might further improve safety (see Outstanding Questions).

Cas9’s “Ship of Theseus paradox”: while Cas9 is emerging as a model for the FDA’s Platform Technology Designation Program for Drug Development, as Cas9 effectors become increasingly customized for their specific therapeutic applications – beyond changes of the gRNA spacer sequences, but including amino acid changes of the Cas9 enzyme to alter PAM, nuclease activity, chimeric addition of different protein domains (themselves often highly modified), or substitution with different Cas9 orthologues either found in nature or generated using AI – at what point do they become too divergent as to warrant additional safety and regulatory scrutiny? In other words how far will be “too far” to fit under the “plausible mechanism” framework for variants that were not included in the clinical trial used for the original approval?

If it is possible to develop a “bespoke” CRISPR-based PGM to correct a unique pathogenic variation, is it also possible for a standard CRISPR therapeutic – with the same spacer and delivery modality – to be similarly “personalized” if a new potential off-target site is identified in a patient’s genome in order to mitigate that risk? Can sites of unwanted mutation not just be identified (nominated) and validated, but also blocked at clinically relevant rates while maintaining therapeutic effectiveness?

In the case of the rs114518452 introducing a novel potential site of mutation for exa-vel CASGEVY, a substitution of the NGG-specific Cas9 effector for one with a more stringent PAM sequence would not likely be able to eliminate unintended edits in those patients: the novel PAM is in sequence context TGGC, while the exa-cel target has a 3’-sequence context of AGGC. Approaches to engineering the NGG PAM of S. pyogenes Cas9 have focused on generating bespoke variants of the sequence NGXX [26], with changes in nucleotide recognition (X) occurring at the 3rd and 4th positions of the PAM. Is the on-demand engineering of Cas9 variants with truly tabula rasa PAMs across larger sequence windows possible to eliminate those potential unwanted interactions?

How do we balance population-level and personalized risk assessment, clinical-grade manufacturability of N-of-1 therapies, the prevalence of different pathogenic genetic variations, motivations of stakeholders, therapy cost, and regulatory pathways be balanced to enable adequate access to patients who could benefit most from these therapies?

How can the extent and distribution of unwanted mutations be determined, monitored, and prevented within a patient? Is there a role for co-administration of anti-CRISPR enzymes as a prophylactic or to decrease the likelihood of unintended editing of germ cells?

How stable are CRISPR cures across spatio-temporal scales? How long do mutations edited in vivo persist in the body? How do those aspects vary depending on cell and tissue type?

K-abe was preclinically evaluated for gene correction efficiency in mice and for safety in nonhuman primates, but it was suggested that cell-based studies would likely be sufficient in the future for other patient-specific gene-editing therapies [3]. This is based on the hypothesis that, for a given treatment modality, substitution of one gRNA for another is not likely to affect the overall safety of the PGM beyond its ability to introduce mutations within a cell. The 20 nt spacer sequence of a gRNA will likely have negligible effects on the overall biodistribution of the PGM [66]. This is also likely true of changes in the amino acids governing PAM recognition in the CRISPR effector.

The concept of CRISPR as a flexible platform, where various CRISPR RNP versions could address different genetic variations of the same disease, has started to shape the regulatory approach to CRISPR therapies. Moving away from the idea that any change in the PGM makes it a completely new therapeutic requiring separate safety evaluations, the FDA released a draft guidance in February 2026 titled “Considerations for the use of the Plausible Mechanism Framework to Develop Individualized Therapies that Target Specific Genetic Conditions with Known Biological Cause” [67]. It was noted that if a genetic disease—caused by multiple variations within a single gene that are clearly linked to the disease—can be treated by a single CRISPR mechanism, then multiple gRNA variants could be included in one IND/BLA; if preclinical and clinical data could be obtained to support the safety and efficacy in the treatment of the disease caused by that collection of mutations, that data would support a “plausible mechanism” that could be used to support the addition of other PGM variants to treat patients with mutations that were not included in the original clinical trial. This scaffolded approach has the potential to expand access of CRISPR therapeutics to those with rare variations of a genetic disease or even to those with rare genetic diseases themselves [66,68].

The widespread adoption of CRISPR biotechnologies is driven by its simple design, whereby a single CRISPR effector could be redirected to different target DNA sequences by modifying spacer sequence in the gRNA. However, as the pace of developments in Cas9 variants (Figure 2A) and delivery accelerates, the field appears to be going back to relying on RNP engineering approaches to address the various challenges in meeting “on-target” efficiencies while eliminating “off-target” risks for each specific therapeutic need across scales (foxes becoming hedgehogs; Figure 3). Indeed, the field seems ripe with opportunities for target-specific optimization of Cas9 RNPs— not just at level of the gRNA’s spacer, mutational modality, or delivery method, but also for optimization of the Cas9 enzyme for activity at that specific sequence; limited interactions with known sequences of potential unwanted interactions in the human genome; cell- and tissue-type optimization; and modulation or attenuation of mediating DDR processes in those cells.

Additionally, the demonstration of the bespoke therapeutic and the emerging regulatory pathways based on the “plausible mechanism” framework raises several interesting questions (see Outstanding Questions) including: if a PGM can be generated on demand for a disease indication with an N = 1, then perhaps, “bespoke” gene editing therapeutics can be personalized after their initial development, as well, to eliminate the edit risks at unwanted sequences by using variants of the CRISPR effector and/or gRNA (Figure 3). A simple example of such an approach, after the in vitro identification of mutation at an unwanted sequence, might be the substitution of one Cas9 effector with another variant that might still recognize the intended target but have altered PAM recognition so that its editing windows no longer include possible recognition of that unwanted sequence: Multiple PAM-variant Cas9 effectors could be included in the original IND/BLA, just as multiple gRNA sequences might. And, in principle, as additional safety and efficacies are demonstrated, this process could draw upon the entire spectrum of CRISPR RNP variants to eliminate interactions at those unique off-target sites. In the future, it is possible that individualized RNPs can be optimized for mutagenic efficiency, personalized for safety based on an individual’s unique DNA, and validated with in vitro safety assays using standardized cellular models that may be generated on demand [9,25,26,53,69] (Figure 3). In short, the road to treat N-of-1 diseases at scale could also lead to individualized CRISPR therapeutics at scale and in parallel. This pathway to personalized CRISPR therapies becomes increasingly possible, particularly for mRNA-based CRISPR therapeutics if it can follow the model of cancer vaccines, where a standard approach to generating clinical grade mRNA can be personalized based on the specific genetics of the patient, with just minor modifications to RNP-encoding mRNA sequences [66,68,70]. Building on these advancements, we are poised to achieve personalized “off-target” elimination or “bespoke modification” after the initial development of a therapeutic for a myriad of genetic diseases.

The factors to consider when describing and evaluating on- and off-target CRISPR activities vary significantly between therapeutic gene editing and non-medical uses.

The meanings of common terminologies — “on-target,” “off-target,” “specificity,” “activity,” and “effectiveness” — shift depending on context.

As we move from describing the biomolecular and biochemical “targeting space” of a CRISPR effector to the “editing window” of a therapeutic, those meanings broaden to encompass cellular, phenotypic, and functional aspects, yet the terms remain constrained by the gene-editing outcomes required for treatment.

As we evaluate gene editing outcomes in tissues, organs, and organ systems—especially when determining the “mutagenic efficiency” of a CRISPR therapy and its “treatment effectiveness” across patients and populations—these terms become more nuanced and less clearly defined.

We consider how there might new opportunities to advance “bespoke” precision genetic medicines (PGM) building on recent developments of CRISPR biotechnologies.
